Lacy's *Gemini Rights* was released July 15 (2022) and was his sophomore album and first on RCA. The breakup is central to it. Lacy has described the record as being about finding himself after a heartbreak, and he framed it as hopeful rather than sad. To me, the subject matter could be sad if you look at it that way, but I feel like it is way more hopeful — and that's the story: finding happiness.

Several sources describe the breakup itself:
- Songfacts reports that Lacy split in November 2021 from a boyfriend of seven months, and that the couple tried to get back together but it didn't work. He told The Guardian he kept trying, and nothing was working.
- The opening track, "Static," was the first song he wrote, about two or three weeks after the split, per his W magazine interview. He said he chose not to run from the pain.
- Lacy told AOL/Billboard-style coverage that the anger was fueled by specific betrayals, including finding his handmade ceramics at his ex's place and learning the ex had lunch with his younger sister to discuss the breakup.
- Lacy said his ex liked the album, though some lines made him pause.

On the creative process, Lacy's Apple Music artist statement says that realizing he isn't separate from his audience made the album feel very easy and fun to make. The GRAMMY.com interview also covers his red flags and why directing his family in a video was "too much" for him, though the excerpt I found didn't include those answers.

Limitations: I only saw excerpts of the W, Guardian, and GRAMMY.com interviews, so I couldn't confirm their full text or any detail about the production process beyond the artist statement.

**Background and release**
- Lacy signed to RCA Records in 2021. He first recorded "Bad Habit" in June 2021, using a beat he made with drums he'd used before. He called writing it a turning point, saying it was "the start of this renaissance of the separation between [past] Steve and [present] Steve." ([GQ, Jeremy Gordon, June 23, 2022](https://www.gq.com/story/gq-hype-steve-lacy))
- After Fousheé heard the instrumental, the two freestyled over it for about 20 minutes, which led to verses and a chorus melody. Lacy later changed the breakdown, drums, and chorus. ([The Guardian, Shaad D'Souza, Dec. 22, 2022](https://www.theguardian.com/music/2022/dec/22/my-mom-thinks-im-doing-drugs-but-im-at-home-baking-cookies-steve-lacy-on-his-breakout-year))
- Lacy said the song was finished a week before he submitted *Gemini Rights* to RCA (same Guardian source).
- It was released June 29, 2022, as the second single from *Gemini Rights* (released July 15, 2022).
- Fan-made sped-up versions went viral on TikTok. RCA later released an official sped-up version, which Lacy initially found "gross" but eventually agreed to (Guardian source above).

**Composition**
- The page describes the track as psychedelic, lo-fi, R&B, bedroom pop, and alt-pop ballad, with many other influences listed.
- Sheet music shows F minor, 84–88 BPM, with vocals from C4 to C6 (cited to Musicnotes). Lacy sings mostly in falsetto.
- The song opens with Fousheé's vocals and has three parts, ending in a stripped-back a cappella section and a "chaotic" jazz fusion breakdown (Los Angeles Times, Aug Brown, Oct. 10, 2022).
- The main instrument is a slightly warped guitar riff, which Paul Tingen says Pogue mixed as the song's main focus (Sound on Sound, Dec. 2022).
- The chorus was changed after a suggestion from Tyler, the Creator, who felt the revised line would "be more memorable" (Billboard Chartbreaker interview, Aug. 3, 2022, [link](https://www.billboard.com/music/features/steve-lacy-bad-habit-billboard-august-2022-chartbreaker-interview-1235121728/)).
- Lacy described the lyrics as "a play on confidence," moving from feeling unworthy to feeling "almost too good" but "still down" (Guardian source above).
- Lacy said the a cappella section was meant to sound like he was "singing directly to" the listener (GQ source above).
- Lacy later told Rolling Stone that the refrain reflected fans wanting something from him that he didn't know about ([Rolling Stone, Jeff Ihaza, Oct. 20, 2022](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/steve-lacy-bad-habit-grammy-preview-1234607474/)).

**Writers and producers**
- Writers (per the page's credits): Steve Lacy, Diana Gordon (wrote part of the ending), John Carroll Kirby, Britanny/Brittany Fousheé (the page uses both spellings), and Matthew Castellanos.
- Producer: Steve Lacy. Lacy also played bass and handled songwriting.
- Kirby is credited with additional synths.
- Mixed by Neal Pogue at his Hot Purple Petting Zoo studio in Los Angeles.
- Mastered by Mike Bozzi at Bernie Grundman Mastering.

**Not in the article:** The Village, Karl Wingate, stems delivery, how the guitar was recorded, and session details are not mentioned.

**Gemini Rights and "Bad Habit" production (article narration)**
- Lacy used several co-writers and producers, musicians, an engineer, and a big-name mixer on *Gemini Rights*. The article does not name them.
- Pogue mixed *Gemini Rights* in his LA studio, HotPurplePettingZoo, which is set up for working in the box.
- Mike Bozzi at Bernie Grundman Mastering mastered *Gemini Rights*.
- The song's sound includes messy-sounding drums, heavy bass, a repetitive guitar part, relatively distant vocals, and a chaotic breakdown.

**Neal Pogue (speaker)**
- On the mix approach: "The focus of 'Bad Habit' is the main guitar, and everything else supports that."
- On the arrangement: The keys "are not really that loud in this song."
- On the process: "I create every mix from scratch because I'm always reaching for something different."
- On album approach: "I look at an album as a TV series, and each song as a different episode."
- On client feedback: Lacy's notes were minimal, such as turning up the guitar or turning down his vocal.

- Main guitar (heavily processed with Waves Infected Mushroom, Waves Scheps 73, Kilohearts Chorus, and UAD API 550A on an aux track)
- Bass (UAD Fairchild, Waves SSL EQ, Waves EV2, McDSP CB101)
- Drums, mainly focused on the kick
- Lead and background vocals (UAD Fairchild 670 on lead vocal; the background vocals received little processing)
- Several synths and a Moog track
- Master bus: Waves L2 and iZotope Ozone

**Lacy's delivery (per article):** Lacy's vocals were not Auto-Tuned, and the article notes his vocals sit in a certain space, not too loud. The article does not describe his deliverables beyond the mix notes above.

The search found that Diana Gordon co-wrote "Bad Habit," but nothing connecting her to "Helmet."

- **Credit:** Gordon is listed as one of the songwriters on "Bad Habit," alongside Lacy, Britanny Fousheé, John Kirby, and Matthew Castellanos. Over the following year, it was changed substantially from its original version and received writing contributions from singers Fousheé and Diana Gordon.
- **Origins:** Songfacts says the song originated in a June 2021 session. Lacy later played Fousheé his demo and the two wrote the melody for the chorus and the verses.
- **Interview:** In a CBS Mornings interview, Lacy played an early version of "Bad Habit," and then tipped his hat to some of the other musicians who were involved with the song, coming up with lyrics and adding synthesizers, naming Fousheé, Gordon, and Kirby.
- **"Helmet":** None of the results mention Gordon or a writing session for "Helmet." One review names "Helmet" as a memorable track on *Gemini Rights*, but gives no credits or session details.

**1. Family members on songs** (Lacy's words, from his answer about directing them)

- "la-la" part on "Helmet": "They sing the "la-la" part on "Helmet.""
- "Mercury" (not used): "They do the "oohs" and "aahs" and the "ba-ba-ba-ba" part on "Mercury," but they were a little pitchy" and "so I couldn't use it."
- "Amber": "I got them on "Amber," singing on the big swell when the bass comes in."
- "Give You The World": "I then added them to "Give You The World," where they're on the "goodbye" part."

Per Lacy, the family appears on three songs. Their "Mercury" parts were cut.

**2. "Edit, edit, edit" and "like how a rapper would"** (Lacy's words, about his creative process)

- "Just blurt words out and vomit them out, let it go, and edit, edit, edit."
- "I would treat [_Gemini Rights_] like how a rapper would and that made it way more fun."

He is describing how he approached making the album: letting ideas come out freely, then editing heavily. "Blurt words out" suggests lyric writing, but the article doesn't state that outright. The rapper comparison is about his approach to this album. It is not a comparison to _Apollo XX1_.

**3. "Sunshine" origin with Fousheé** (Lacy's words)

- Fousheé brought the hook: "she just had this hook and we were harmonizing for a moment on that part. It became the chorus."
- Lacy then asked her to be the album's only feature: "Just be the only feature on my album."
- It came from a freestyle process, with the two singing into two mics. It "'d get up to about 20 minutes long" before being trimmed.

**4. _Apollo XX1_ and working alone** (Writer's words, not Lacy's)

- "is an even more personal offering than his 2019 debut solo effort, _Apollo XX1_"
- "Majorly self-produced by Lacy"

The article spells the title "Apollo XX1," not "XXI." The writer contrasts _Gemini Rights_ with _Apollo XX1_ only on how personal the album is. Lacy doesn't discuss working alone on _Apollo XX1_. His only "independent" remark is "I was really happy being independent for a while," which refers to his earlier label situation. Otherwise, the article emphasizes collaboration, especially with Fousheé and his family.
